newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Opposition says Russia is leaderless.
newsitem.headline: Opposition says Russia is leaderless.

text.p: Opposition leaders, addressing parliament's first full session since President Boris Yeltsin announced he would have heart surgery, said on Wednesday Russia was leaderless and demanded action to stop the rot.

"If the car is smashed up and the driver is in hospital, you should change the car and the driver," extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky told the opposition-dominated State Duma, or lower house, at the start of its autumn session.

He and other opposition leaders painted a picture of chaos and confusion in Yeltsin's absence, sharpening their claws for what promises to be an autumn of battles with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government and the Kremlin.

Yeltsin, 65, announced on September 5 that he would have a heart operation and has been in hospital since September 13. Aides say he is working a maximum of three hours a day as he prepares for a bypass operation due in six to 10 weeks time.
Yeltsin met Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the Middle East and Afghanistan.

A proposal by Yeltsin for the 12-state Commonwealth of Independent States, set up on the ashes of the Soviet Union in 1991, to discuss the situation in Afghanistan bore fruit. The meeting was expected to go ahead in Kazakhstan on Friday.
The president also sent a message to the Duma asking for "significantly" better and more intensive work.

Previous sessions have been marred by fights between deputies, battles of will with Yeltsin and the passing of few laws, and Thursday is the third anniversary of a rebellion by the old parliament which Yeltsin put down with tanks.

The new parliamentary session is likely to be dominated by a struggle with the government over its budget plans, which need Duma approval to become law, and by demands for the government to pay off months of unpaid wages to millions of workers.
Deputies laid down the gauntlet by inviting Chernomyrdin to address the Duma on the social and economic situation on Friday.
The prime minister, who has resisted calls to loosen purse strings to cut inflation and satisfy foreign creditors, says matters are in hand and has refused similar demands in the past.

"The government is unable to resolve a single question," said Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, who heads the most powerful opposition force. "If things go on like this Russia will repeat the fate of the Soviet Union."
Zyuganov proposed a Council of State be set up, grouping leaders of the main political and national security bodies, to examine the country's problems and decide what should be done.
He said the council should comprise members of both houses of parliament, government leaders and representatives from the Defence and Security Councils headed by Yeltsin.

Zyuganov did not specifically repeat demands for Yeltsin to resign and kept under wraps his party's plans for a medical commission to be created to check the health of top state officials -- a move which might force Yeltsin out of office.
Yeltsin's liberal opponents also attacked the government's record and called for changes.

Grigory Yavlinsky, head of the liberal Yabloko faction, said that in Yeltsin's absence there were clear policy contradictions between Chernomyrdin, security tsar Alexander Lebed and Anatoly Chubais, head of the Kremlin administration.

In a blow to Yeltsin's authority, the latest monthly poll of political experts by the Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper showed the president, who usually leads the ratings, was currently rated only as Russia's third most influential politician. Chernomyrdin led the poll, ahead of Lebed.
